newsitem.title: ROMANIA: President upbeat about Romania joining NATO next.
newsitem.headline: President upbeat about Romania joining NATO next.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu said on Wednesday NATO leaders had assured him that his country and Slovenia, passed over for the Alliance's first expansion, were "certain candidates" for admission next time.
But to secure membership, Romania had to press on with its newly-launched market reforms.

"They told me that in 1999, when NATO celebrates its 50th anniversary, the alliance will expand again and that there are two certain candidates for that enlargement -- Romania and Slovenia," he said in a live television interview from Madrid.
"Of course -- if we keep up the pace of reform."
"What we obtained was virtually the maximum that could be obtained at this moment," he said.
NATO decided at its two-day summit in Madrid to take in only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic as its first ex-communist members.
But Constantinescu said the Romanians had "emerged as winners (in Madrid) as discussions concentrated on Romania and Slovenia".

He said France's President Jacques Chirac and other European leaders had lobbied intensely on Romania's behalf in the hours before the final decision to admit only three new members for now, as the United States had demanded.
"With his usual chivalry, President Chirac told me that...starting with President (Bill) Clinton, all the leaders had only words of praise for Romania."

He invited Romanians to turn out to greet him and Clinton when the U.S. President's paid a lightning visit to Bucharest on Friday -- intended to sweeten the NATO pill and encourage Romanians to press on with their reform efforts.
"See you in University Square, the symbol of our great sacrifice for freedom and democracy," he said.

University Square is the place in central Bucharest where students were shot dead during Romania's 1989 anti-communist revolution. Clinton's address to Romanians in the square will be the highlight of his eight-hour visit.
Constantinescu had earlier said he hoped the first visit by a U.S. leader in more than 20 years would "mark the beginning of a strategic Romanian-U.S. partnership".

He said the seven months since he and a centrist alliance ousted ex-communists in presidential and parliamentary polls had not been enough to close the reform gap separating Romania from the three more advanced ex-communist states.
"Romania only had seven months of extraordinary progress, while the others had seven years," he said.
Former prime minister Petre Roman, now the second-ranking official in the state as chairman of the upper house of parliament, praised France's efforts on Bucharest's behalf.
"France, first and foremost, through the firm voice of President Chirac, as well as Italy, Spain and Portugal, supported Romania's bid in an exemplary way," he said.
Constantinescu said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had also promised to be "a strong supporter of Romania's Euro-Atlantic and European integration".
